phonemes.desc: Palatal glide [j], as in English 'yes' — the name begins with the sound that opens 'yard'.
Open-mid rounded [ɔ] with nasal colouring, rolled r, and voiced dental fricative [ð] as in 'this'.

pronunciation.approximation: YORTH — the first sound is English 'y', the vowel the open 'o' of 'thought', and the name ends on the voiced 'th' of 'this'.

kin.label: Proto-Germanic
kin.form: *erþō, 'earth' — the root survives in Old English eorþe (English 'earth') and Gothic airþa

kin.label: Eddic bynames
kin.form: Fjǫrgyn and Hlóðyn — the other names under which the skalds invoke Þórr's mother (Skáldskaparmál); whether they are hers or separate goddesses, the sources never say

kin.label: Norse kin
kin.form: Daughter of Anarr and Nótt (Night), wife of Óðinn, mother of Þórr — the genealogy given in Gylfaginning ch. 9

pronunciation.note: Jǫrð is Tier 1: the ǫ and the ð are distinctive letters that ASCII flattens entirely — 'jord' loses the nasalised vowel and the voiced fricative of the Old Norse name.

domains.title: Earth
domains.subtitle: Earth, Mother of Thor
domains.lead: Jǫrð is the Norse earth — not a character with adventures but the ground itself personified: daughter of Night, wife of Óðinn, and mother of Þórr, the mightiest of the gods. The skalds need no stories about her; they call the very land by her name, and every thunder-clap is her son walking.

cards.name: The Earth
cards.desc: Her domain is the ground itself — fields, mountains, graves; she is the oldest of the ásynjur because everything stands on her.

cards.name: Earth Mother of Þórr
cards.desc: By Óðinn she bears Þórr, strongest of the gods — the storm literally born of the earth (Gylfaginning ch. 9; Skáldskaparmál).

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Jǫrð recovers the ǫ and ð that plain ASCII jord flattens; the restoration is the name as the skalds wrote it.

cards.name: In the Eddas
cards.desc: Listed among the ásynjur and invoked in kennings — 'son of Jǫrð' is Þórr's standard style from Bragi to the late skalds.

symbols.name: The land itself
symbols.meaning: She needs no emblem: in skaldic kennings the ground is her body, and 'the meal of Jǫrð' is a kenning for the dust of the earth

symbols.name: Þórr
symbols.meaning: Her son by Óðinn: the thunder-god's strength is earth-strength, and 'Jǫrð's son' is among his commonest titles

symbols.name: Fjǫrgyn and Hlóðyn
symbols.meaning: Her twin names in the poetry — Völuspá calls the thunderer 'Hlóðyn's glorious son' (v. 56) — three masks for a single mother

symbols.name: The dark lineage
symbols.meaning: As daughter of Anarr and Nótt (Night) she belongs to the old giant layer of the cosmos, older than Óðinn's race

mythology.lead: Jǫrð has no saga of her own — the Norse sources never give her a deed. Her 'myths' are her genealogy, her marriage, her three names, and the silence where her temple should be; read together they are the Norse answer to the question of what the ground is.

myths.title: Daughter of Night
myths.text: The Prose Edda (Gylfaginning ch. 9–10) gives Jǫrð the strangest pedigree in the pantheon: she is the daughter of Anarr and Nótt — of Anarr and Night. Her mother Nótt is the giantess who drives the black chariot across the night sky, ancestress of every dawn; her father Anarr is little more than a name in the margin. From Night comes the earth, and from Night also comes Dagr, Day, born of the bright Dellingr — so the earth's brother is daylight itself, and the two are ever turning over the same horizon. The genealogy is a compact cosmology stated as a family tree: darkness precedes and engenders both the ground we stand on and the light that crosses it. When the skalds called Þórr kin of Nótt they were keeping the whole system inside one kenning — the thunder's pedigree runs back past Óðinn to the Night that came before the gods.

myths.title: Wife of Óðinn, Mother of Þórr
myths.text: Snorri lists Jǫrð among Óðinn's wives — Gylfaginning ch. 9 names her in the tally of nine — and the whole mythology leans on the match. Their son is Þórr, strongest of the gods, and the skalds' standard style for him is the double patronymic: son of Óðinn and of Jǫrð. The union is the Norse sky-father/earth-mother formula compressed into a single household — the storm is literally what happens when heaven touches ground. Nowhere do the sources narrate the courtship, and none is needed: this is not a love story but a standing fact, like gravity. Þórr's hammer-fall is the marriage still being consummated; every thunderstorm is the myth told again in weather, and the skalds, who never tired of the kenning, understood that a formula repeated a thousand times is a cult.

myths.title: Fjǫrgyn and Hlóðyn
myths.text: Þórr's mother wears three names. The skaldic handbook Skáldskaparmál lists the thunderer as son of Óðinn and of Jǫrð, Fjǫrgyn, and Hlóðyn — and Völuspá (v. 56) calls him 'Hlóðyn's glorious son' at the world's end, when he strides out to meet the wolf. Whether Fjǫrgyn and Hlóðyn are bynames of Jǫrð or older, separate earth-goddesses folded into her by the skalds, the sources never say; Cleasby–Vigfusson treats Fjǫrgyn as an earth-goddess in her own right, and the element's own meaning is disputed (mountain? the living world?) — fitting for a name whose owner is disputed too. The three-name pattern is the tradition's honest way of admitting that the earth is one goddess wearing as many faces as terrain: field, fell, and the grave-dark loam. Þórr, asked, could have named three mothers; the skalds answered for him by never choosing.

myths.title: The Cult That Is Everywhere
myths.text: No temple of Jǫrð is recorded anywhere in the Norse world — no altar, no image, no dedication — and the silence is the loudest thing the sources say about her. Worship of the earth ran beneath cult rather than through it: the graves were dug into her, the fields cut out of her, every hof stood on her, and the first gesture of the rites was to face or touch the ground. The law approached her the only way law can — as the commons, the unowned ground and the open pathways that belong to everyone, which is to say to the earth herself. Her 'temple' is thus the entire archaeological record of the North: every longhouse floor, every barrow, every field-wall. A goddess without a sanctuary is not a forgotten goddess; she is the one sanctuary everything is built in, and the North never stopped holding services.

lore.syncretism: Jǫrð's closest relative is Tacitus' Nerthus, the Terra Mater whose wagon processed among the Germanic tribes (Germania ch. 40) — the same earth-mother function on the mainland, though the sources never equate the names. Medieval Icelanders, translating classical texts, rendered Gaia and Tellus as Jǫrð, making her the Norse face of the universal earth-mother, an equation that survived into the scholarly Latin of the Edda commentaries. Modern reception has been generous and careless by turns: Marvel's comics make Thor the son of Gaea and the films of Frigga, splitting the ancient sky-father/earth-mother pairing into two rival cosmologies, while modern Heathenry restores Jǫrð herself to worship, blót and all — the rare case where a goddess' cult was revived not from archaeology but from grammar, her name having never stopped meaning 'earth.'
lore.culturalLegacy: Jǫrð never died because she never lived anywhere but underfoot. Her name is the ordinary word for earth in Icelandic, Norwegian, Danish, and Swedish jord; English 'earth' descends from her Old English cognate eorþe. 'Mother Earth' — the phrase behind Earth Day, Gaia theory, and a whole modern environmental iconography — is, linguistically, Jǫrð's daughter. In Scandinavia her name has returned as a given name, and in Ásatrú blot she receives the first or final pouring, for the oldest reason: every rite that happens on the ground happens on her. Even her son's weekday carries the lineage quietly into English — Þórr's day, Thursday, is her family name worn by the calendar.
lore.extendedMeditation: Jǫrð is the goddess who needs no biography. The Norse sources give her no adventure, no speech, no conflict — only a genealogy, a marriage, and a son; and then, in the kennings, something better than deeds: a body that is the world. To call the land 'Jǫrð' is to keep a person in the grammar of geography, to refuse the idea that the ground is dead matter. Her marriage to Óðinn is the oldest cosmological sentence in the language — the sky bestrides the earth, and the child of their union is the storm, Þórr, whose hammer-crash is the sound of his parents still touching. And her three names are the tradition's confession that the earth is one goddess wearing as many faces as terrain. A goddess without a temple is not a forgotten goddess. She is the one temple everything is built in.

sources.name: Cleasby-Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, s.v. jörð, Fjörgyn

lore.archaeology: Jǫrð has no temple, altar, or image, and that absence is itself the archaeological fact: no site in Scandinavia can be assigned to her cult, and even the great wagon procession of the earth-goddess described by Tacitus (Germania ch. 40) belongs to Nerthus, her continental Germanic cousin, not to Jǫrð by name. The closest material kin are the procession finds of the Vendel and Viking periods — wagons and horse-gear that belong to the vanir cult Tacitus describes. What can be dated is her son: runestones across Scandinavia invoke Þórr (the ninth-century Rök stone calls on Þórr for protection), and the skaldic corpus keeps her name in constant grammatical use — jǫrð, 'earth' — down to every modern Scandinavian tongue. Her monument is the land itself and the language that never stopped naming it.
